Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) predominantly use paper-based systems for recording patient data. Community health workers collect data on paper forms, which facilities collate into paper reports on program outcomes, stock, and surveillance. These are sent to health zones for entry into the national DHIS2 (SNIS) platform.DHIS2 DRC Data Use Decentralized digital entry at facilities is rare, limited to some large sites with reliable power/internet; most entry is centralized at zones due to infrastructure deficits.DHIS2 DRC Data Use TB data from 2061 centers follows this: paper forms validated at centers, forwarded to zones for DHIS2.DHIS2 DRC Data Use Isolated pilots (e.g., donor laptops in 63 facilities) succeeded briefly but failed post-funding due to maintenance issues.DHIS2 DRC Data Use No widespread EMR; some OpenMRS pilots exist but not scaled to majority rural clinics.OpenMRS EMR4All Barriers: poor electricity/internet, funding, skills, outdated paper tools. National DHIS2 (since 2013) excels in aggregate reporting (80%+ completeness), but rural point-of-care remains paper, causing transcription errors. Policy ambition for digital UHC contrasts with rural paper reality.

revision_notes: Original cited sources (dhis2.org overview, childhealthtaskforce PDF, stoptb TB assessment) were fetched/read and support a largely paper-based baseline, but pre-date more recent facility-level pilots. Fresh searches turned up fetched, read evidence of genuine point-of-care digital data capture: an RTI/CDC-supported eIDSR pilot gave tablets to head/assistant nurses in 235 responsible health centres and hospitals across 15 of 27 health zones in Haut-Katanga province, entering data directly into DHIS2 from October 2022 (RTI working paper, 2024); a peer-reviewed 2025 study found SORMAS piloted for facility-level case entry in 29 health centres plus 1 hospital in Kenge health zone, Kwango province (2022-2024); and the IASO/SSC community care site app, syncing to DHIS2, has scaled to all 26 provinces for community health worker reporting (Bluesquare, June 2026). These are still minority practices relative to the great majority of rural clinics nationwide, which continue to rely on paper forms consolidated at health-zone level, but they represent real, verified digital data capture at a meaningful number of facilities. This moves the score from 1 (Entirely paper) to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital). This is not a promotion to the top of the scale (4), so no human_review flag applies.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in the Democratic Republic of the Congo remain predominantly paper-based for point-of-care data capture, with nurses and community health workers completing paper registers and weekly epidemiological report forms that are physically or verbally relayed to the health zone office for entry into the national DHIS2 (SNIS) platform. A minority of facilities now capture data digitally at the point of care: an electronic Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (eIDSR) system using Android tablets connected to DHIS2 has been used by nurses in 235 health centres and hospitals across 15 of 27 health zones in Haut-Katanga province since October 2022, the SORMAS case-management system has been piloted for direct facility-level entry in health centres in Kenge health zone, Kwango province, and the IASO/SSC mobile application, which syncs to DHIS2, is used nationally by community health workers across all 26 provinces to report community-level health data. These digital tools remain confined to specific programmes and provinces rather than standard practice, and the great majority of rural clinics nationwide continue to rely on paper-based recording.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (PNC) record criminal cases and complaints primarily through paper-based procès-verbaux (official statements/reports for findings, arrests, hearings, etc.). These documents are generally typed but hearings are handwritten in most cases, with strict formal requirements for validity (e.g., signed, dated). No evidence of digital case management systems at rural level; procedures rely on written complaints and manual OPJ processes. Recent HRIS is for personnel management only, not cases. UN tools like goCASE used by MONUSCO, not PNC. Reforms emphasize training/accountability, not digital recording. Rural infrastructure likely precludes digital adoption.

revision_notes: Original cited sources were fetched and read. The ecoi.net IRB report (2023) confirms that police reports (procès-verbaux) are typed or handwritten paper documents subject to strict formal legal requirements, with no mention of digital case recording. The Coginta HRIS article and goCASE description were also fetched: HRIS covers personnel/career management only (not case data), and goCASE is a UN tool used by MONUSCO, not the PNC, so neither evidences digitisation of case records. Fresh searches (2024-2025) found further fetched evidence: an ACP report (October 2024) on computer equipment (32 computers, 16 tablets, 7 printers, 5 servers) delivered to the General Inspectorate (IGPNC) central office in Kinshasa and its four provincial antennae (Haut-Katanga, North Kivu, South Kivu, Kasaï-Oriental), intended for audit/investigation database use by inspectors, and a further Coginta article (June 2025) confirming the HRIS now also equips HR departments at the provincial police stations of Tshikapa, Bunia and Mbandaka. Both concern oversight/inspection and personnel administration at central or provincial-capital level, not case recording at ordinary rural police stations. No evidence of digital case-recording adoption at rural stations was found; the score of 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural police stations in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continue to record criminal cases and complaints entirely through paper-based procès-verbaux (official statements), which are generally typed, though hearings are recorded by hand in most cases, and must meet strict formal legal requirements to be valid. Recent digitisation initiatives are confined to personnel administration and central oversight rather than case recording: a Human Resources Information System introduced under the EU-funded PARP 3 police reform programme now covers career and staffing management for the national police, including at the provincial police stations of Tshikapa, Bunia and Mbandaka, and the General Inspectorate of the Police received computer equipment in 2024 for its central Kinshasa office and four provincial antennae to support internal audit and investigation databases. Neither initiative extends to the day-to-day recording of criminal cases and complaints at rural police stations, which remains an entirely manual, paper-based process.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (877 out of 979 local offices) record births using entirely paper-based carbon copy registers with four copies per event: one to applicant, one to local court, one to central office in Kinshasa, one retained locally. No computers or mobile technology used in the registration process. Accessibility challenges in rural areas exacerbate low registration rates, but recording remains manual. Recent pilots (e.g., Masina urban) and plans for historical digitization exist, but no evidence of digital recording in rural facilities as of 2019 reports; national digital plans (2026+) do not yet impact rural registries.

revision_notes: Original cited APAI-CRVS snapshot was fetched and confirms the paper-based, four-copy carbon register system, though the underlying data dates to 2019; FamilySearch wiki (not re-fetched this round) is a general secondary source consistent with this. Fresh searches found and fetched a June 2025 UNFPA article confirming a joint UN pilot (UNICEF, BCNUDH, UNHCR, UNFPA) issuing digital tablets to registry staff in the commune of Masina, Kinshasa, to digitise birth registration data entry, alongside references to a national Digital Code (2023) and National Digital Plan (2025). Search snippets (not independently fetched) also indicate a similar 2022 population-register pilot in the commune of Kintambo (Kinshasa) and a June 2024 training/tablet distribution linking birth registration to vaccination records in Matadi, Kongo Central. All identified digitisation activity is confined to specific urban or peri-urban pilot communes; no evidence was found of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices. The score of 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed for rural registries specifically.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continue to record births, deaths and marriages using entirely paper-based, four-copy carbon registers, with one copy retained locally, one sent to the local court, one to the central office in Kinshasa, and one given to the applicant; no computers or mobile devices are used in the registration process itself. Digitisation activity to date is confined to pilot programmes in specific Kinshasa communes, notably a joint UN-backed pilot launched in Masina in 2025 that issued digital tablets to registry staff to capture birth registration data, following an earlier population-register pilot in Kintambo from 2022. These initiatives have not extended to rural registry offices, which continue to operate the manual paper-based process described in national civil registration and vital statistics assessments.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in DRC predominantly use paper-based registers for recording attendance, enrollment, and administrative data. School directors complete printed questionnaires for the national statistical yearbook, sent and returned physically by ground transport, leading to low response rates, delays, and reliance on estimates due to losses and poor infrastructure, especially in rural areas. No evidence of routine digital data entry at the point of service; EMIS efforts focus on national/provincial aggregation and decentralized planning (e.g., UNICEF-supported decentralized EMIS, Cordaid's GPS-mapped database combining existing sources), not school-level digital tools. SECOPE maintains a centralized (insecure) digital payroll database, but schools handle paper files. Barriers include poor ICT infrastructure, electricity/connectivity deficits in rural areas (e.g., only 7% rural schools with electricity per recent WB analysis), logistical challenges, and lack of devices/training. National SSEF policy aspires to EMIS dashboards, but rural reality remains manual recording with upward paper transcription, unchanged as of 2017-2024 reports.

revision_notes: The World Bank working paper (September 2024) on digital readiness of DRC schools was fetched and read; it confirms severe rural ICT/electricity infrastructure gaps (around 7% of rural schools with electricity access) and supports a continued paper-based reality at school level, and is the most current and authoritative of the four originally cited sources. The rescue.org, IICBA and ReliefWeb sources were not re-fetched this round but are older, general, and consistent with the World Bank finding. Fresh searches surfaced two further Ministry of Education digital initiatives (a 2023 national school geolocation platform, and KoboToolbox-based enumerator surveys building a nationwide school database) but these are periodic external mapping/census exercises carried out by enumerators with tablets, not routine digital data capture by school staff at the point of service, so they do not evidence a change in the facility-level recording practice the variable measures. The score of 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continue to rely on paper-based registers and printed questionnaires to record attendance, enrolment and administrative data, which are transported physically to provincial and central offices for compilation into national education statistics. Severe infrastructure constraints, including electricity access at only around 7% of rural schools, continue to preclude routine digital record-keeping at the point of service. Ministry of Education digitisation efforts, such as a national school geolocation platform and enumerator-led tablet-based school censuses, involve periodic external data collection exercises rather than day-to-day digital data capture by school staff, so administrative and attendance recording within rural primary schools remains an entirely manual, paper-based process.
